--- Page 1 ---
Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and
Costly Preemption
JIAHUI NI, Purdue University, USA
VISHRANT TRIPATHI, Purdue University, USA
Modeling inference workloads for transformer-based neural networks poses unique challenges due to their
dynamic memory footprints, head-of-line blocking caused by heavy-tailed request distributions, and memory-
dependent preemption overhead arising from the need to load/unload cache state. In this paper, we introduce
a new queuing model that captures the impacts of these features on system stability and scheduling design.
We show that the Gittins-index policy, which minimizes mean response time in the standard M/G/1 setting,
can incur substantial preemption overhead in our model. Motivated by this limitation, we propose the Multi-
Level-Priority-Threshold (MLPT) policy, that limits preemption while preserving priority for short jobs. We
characterize the mean response time under MLPT and provide empirical rules-of-thumb to solve the resulting
threshold-optimization problem. Our key observation is that optimal scheduling is a balance between reducing
the response times of shorter jobs and limiting the overhead incurred when preemption occurs. These results
provide a theoretical framework for understanding scheduling in memory constrained queuing systems for
inference tasks.
1
Introduction
Transformer-based inference is becoming a major contributor to traffic growth in large-scale in-
frastructure and compute serving systems. Over the past three decades, traditional performance
modeling and queuing literature has served the computing infrastructure community well in ana-
lyzing the fundamental limits of system performance and in designing more efficient architectures.
However, modern inference workloads have characteristics that are not captured by classical queu-
ing models. In particular, inference requests can have highly variable and often unknown execution
times, their memory footprints can grow substantially as they are served, and interrupting a request
can incur significant overhead because the state accumulated during execution must be moved
or reconstructed. These characteristics couple scheduling decisions with memory occupancy and
service capacity in ways that are fundamentally different from conventional compute workloads.
A particularly important characteristic of transformer inference is its dynamically growing
memory footprint. During autoregressive generation, a request maintains a Key-Value (KV) cache
that grows with the generated sequence length. Consequently, the memory required by a request
increases with its attained service: a request that has been served for a long time may occupy
substantially more memory than a newly arrived request. Modern LLM serving systems have
developed sophisticated mechanisms to manage this memory. For example, continuous batching
allows requests to enter and leave a batch at iteration granularity [1], while PagedAttention
improves KV-cache memory utilization by reducing fragmentation through paged allocation [2].
However, these mechanisms do not eliminate the finite capacity of GPU memory. When the available
KV-cache capacity is exhausted, requests may need to be preempted and their state transferred
to host memory or reconstructed through recomputation, introducing additional data-movement
and computational overhead. Thus, memory is not merely a resource that determines how many
requests can be simultaneously admitted: as memory pressure increases, it can directly affect how
efficiently inference work is completed.
This distinction is important because a finite memory constraint can change the service process
of a request. Consider a request whose memory footprint grows with its attained service. While
Authors’ Contact Information: Jiahui Ni, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA, ni169@purdue.edu; Vishrant
Tripathi, Purdue University, West Lafayette, Indiana, USA, tripathv@purdue.edu.

Jiahui Ni and Vishrant Tripathi
its memory requirement remains below the available capacity, it can be served at its nominal rate.
Once its footprint reaches the memory capacity, however, the remaining computation may have to
be performed under memory pressure, resulting in a lower effective service rate. The amount of
work affected by this slowdown depends on the intrinsic size of the request and on how its memory
footprint evolves during execution. Long requests are therefore affected disproportionately: they
are more likely to reach the memory limit and, once they do, may spend a significant fraction of
their execution in the slower regime. This creates an interaction between job size, attained service,
memory occupancy, and effective service capacity that is absent from the standard 𝑀/𝐺/1 model.
Memory constraints also fundamentally change the cost of preemption. Preemption is attractive
for inference workloads because request sizes are generally unknown upon arrival and can exhibit
substantial variability. Under FCFS scheduling, a long request can cause significant head-of-line
blocking for shorter requests, motivating scheduling policies that prioritize requests according
to their attained service [3, 4]. In a classical 𝑀/𝐺/1 queue, such policies can exploit preemption
without explicitly accounting for the cost of switching between jobs. In inference serving, however,
preempting a request can require removing its accumulated KV cache from fast memory and
subsequently restoring that state through data movement or recomputation. Because the amount of
cached state grows with attained service, the cost of preemption itself can increase as a request runs.
Thus, aggressive preemption can improve response time by reducing head-of-line blocking while
simultaneously consuming additional system capacity through state movement or reconstruction.
Existing serving systems mitigate these costs through mechanisms such as proactive KV-cache
swapping and live request migration [5, 6], but the fundamental scheduling tradeoff remains.
The resulting problem is also distinct from classical queuing models with finite buffers. In a
finite-buffer queue, the capacity constraint limits the amount of queued work that can be stored
in the system; when the buffer is full, newly arriving jobs may be blocked or dropped, while
the service process of a job already in service is unaffected. In contrast, the memory constraint
considered here is coupled to the execution of the job itself. A request can progressively increase
its memory footprint while receiving service, reach the finite memory capacity during execution,
and subsequently experience a reduced service rate. Moreover, if the request is preempted, its
accumulated memory state determines the additional work required to resume it. The capacity
constraint therefore affects not only admission or occupancy, but also the service requirement of a
job and the cost of scheduling decisions.
This distinction becomes increasingly important as inference is deployed across large-scale
infrastructure as well as resource-constrained edge and on-device environments. At the edge and
on end devices, available high-speed memory is much more limited, while moving state between
memory hierarchies or between processing units can consume a larger fraction of the available
computational and communication capacity. Consequently, memory pressure and state movement
can have an even more pronounced effect on effective inference capacity in such environments.
1.1
Contributions
In this work, we introduce the 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queue, a new queuing model for inference workloads
with dynamically growing memory footprints, finite memory capacity, memory-dependent service
degradation, and nonzero preemption overhead (see Figure 1). The model retains the basic structure
of the classical 𝑀/𝐺/1 queue while explicitly capturing the interactions between attained service,
memory occupancy, service rate, and preemption cost. Specifically, a job with attained service
𝑎occupies memory according to a nondecreasing function 𝑔(𝑎); the system has finite memory
capacity 𝐶; service proceeds at a reduced rate 𝛽once the memory requirement exceeds 𝐶; and
preempting a job incurs additional work proportional to its accumulated memory state.


--- Page 3 ---
Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
3
We use this model to study both the fundamental stability implications of memory constraints and
the scheduling tradeoffs created by costly preemption. For non-preemptive policies, we characterize
the stability region and show how memory-induced service degradation introduces additional
load that depends on the portion of a job served beyond the memory threshold. For preemptive
scheduling, we show that the classical Gittins-index policy, which minimizes mean response time
in the standard 𝑀/𝐺/1 setting, can incur substantial preemption overhead in the presence of
memory-dependent switching costs. Motivated by this observation, we propose a Multi-Level-
Priority-Threshold (MLPT) policy that limits preemption while retaining priority for jobs with
small attained service. We derive the mean response time under MLPT and characterize the
resulting threshold optimization problem, revealing how the tradeoff between scheduling gain and
preemption overhead depends on memory capacity and the cost of restoring state.
1.2
Related Work
LLM Serving Systems. Recent works have developed a range of system-level techniques to improve
the throughput and latency of LLM serving, including continuous batching [1], chunked prefill [7],
and prefill-decode disaggregation [8]. Efficient memory management is similarly critical because
autoregressive generation requires a KV cache that grows with sequence length; PagedAttention
[2] improves GPU-memory utilization by reducing KV-cache fragmentation, while systems such
as FastServe [5] and Llumnix [6] use preemption, KV-cache swapping, and live migration to
mitigate latency and load-imbalance under memory pressure. Nevertheless, request sizes can
vary substantially, making FCFS-like scheduling susceptible to head-of-line blocking [3, 4], while
preemption and KV-cache management introduce state-dependent overhead and memory pressure
can reduce the effective serving rate. These systems primarily address these challenges through
system design and optimization; our work provides a complementary queuing-theoretic analysis of
scheduling when memory footprints grow during service and both service rate and preemption
cost depend on the attained service of a job.
Queuing Analysis. Queuing theory provides a rich framework for latency-oriented scheduling in
𝑀/𝐺/1 queues. Since LLM request sizes are generally unknown upon arrival, inference can naturally
be viewed as scheduling with unknown job sizes, for which the Gittins index policy minimizes mean
response time under costless preemption [9, 10]. However, optimal scheduling with preemption
overhead remains an open problem [11], and switching costs can invalidate conventional Gittins-
type index policies [12]. Closer to our work, different variations of the preemption overhead setting
have been analyzed in the 𝑀/𝐺/1 queue over the years including class-based priority [13], and
preemptive-repeats with both LIFO scheduling [14, 15] and age-dependent scheduling [16, 17].
However, these works do not consider memory constraints or settings where the preemption
overhead itself is age-dependent.
In standard 𝑀/𝐺/1 settings, it has been shown that the Gittins Index policy can be translated
into simpler scheduling disciplines [18–20] with threshold-type structure. Our proposed MLPT
policy is motivated by these threshold-type structures and the idea of preemption checkpointing,
introduced in [21] to tackle costly preemptions. Classical methods like multilevel-feedback-queues
(MLFQ) [22] provide a practical way to implement such threshold-based prioritization. Crucially,
existing analysis and scheduling policies do not capture the coupling between attained service,
growing memory footprint, service degradation, and preemption cost that arises in our model.
Theoretical Modeling for LLM Inference. The closest line of work related to ours is the growing
body of literature on theoretical modeling for LLM inference. Recent studies incorporate increas-
ingly detailed aspects of batching and KV-cache constraints, including request-level batching
[23], iteration-level batching and token-budget constraints [24], dynamically growing KV-cache
occupancy under finite GPU memory [25], and memory-constrained multi-stage execution with


--- Page 4 ---
4
Jiahui Ni and Vishrant Tripathi
Fig. 1. 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queuing model
dynamic iteration times [26, 27]. These works establish stability, throughput, or asymptotic latency
guarantees, but do not provide an explicit steady-state characterization of mean response time
under preemptive scheduling with memory-dependent overhead. Unlike existing LLM-specific
models, our approach connects these memory effects directly to classical latency-oriented analysis
and scheduling design.
2
System Model
We introduce a memory-constrained queuing model for preemptive scheduling with dynamically
growing memory footprints, finite memory capacity, and nonzero preemption overhead, which we
denote by 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽. The model retains the basic structure of a classical 𝑀/𝐺/1 queue, but differs
from it in three key aspects: (i) the memory footprint of a job grows as a function 𝑔(·) depending
on its attained service; (ii) the server has a finite memory capacity 𝐶, and once this capacity is
exceeded, the service rate slows down by a factor 𝛽; and (iii) preempting a job incurs an additional
switching cost proportional to the memory it occupies.
Throughout, we assume that, until the memory constraint is reached, the server processes jobs
at a normalized rate of 1. Jobs arrive according to a Poisson process with rate 𝜆. Let 𝐿denote the
intrinsic size of a job, i.e., the amount of service required to complete the job when it is processed
continuously at the normalized service rate of one and incurs no preemption overhead. Job sizes are
i.i.d. according to distribution 𝐹𝐿(ℓ) with density 𝑓𝐿(ℓ). We consider the classical zero-information
setting, in which the scheduler knows the distribution 𝐹𝐿but does not know the realization of 𝐿
for an individual job upon arrival.
The 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽model is motivated by inference for transformer-based neural networks. In this
setting, a job corresponds to an inference request, its size corresponds to the total amount of decode
work, and its attained service corresponds to the amount of decoding completed so far. We focus
on the decode phase and assume that at most one request is served at a time, so that the underlying
queuing structure remains single-server. The model can be extended to 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/𝑘𝐶
𝛽queues to capture
batching, when 𝑘decode-phase requests are processed in parallel.
2.1
Dynamic Memory Footprint
In our 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽model, a job occupies an amount of memory that increases with its attained service.
Let 𝑗denote the job currently in service, and let 𝑎𝑗(𝑡) denote the attained service of job 𝑗at time
𝑡. We assume that at most one job is served at a time, and only the memory of the running job
is retained in the server. Let 𝑔: R+ →R+ be a known monotonically non-decreasing function
characterizing the memory requirement as a function of attained service. Then, the memory

𝑀(𝑡) = 𝑔␀𝑎𝑗(𝑡) .

For transformer-based inference, this state corresponds to the KV cache accumulated during
autoregressive decoding. As decoding progresses, each newly generated token contributes additional
KV states that must be retained for future attention computation. The function 𝑔(·) captures the
general behavior of KV cache growth. When a standard full-attention transformer is used, the KV
cache size grows approximately linearly with the generated sequence length, which corresponds to
𝑔(𝑎) = 𝛼𝜇𝑎, where the parameter 𝛼captures the memory growth associated with each generated
token, and 𝜇captures the rate of token generation.

rate to one while the memory footprint of the running job remains within the capacity 𝐶. Once the
memory requirement exceeds this capacity, the service rate is reduced to 𝛽, where 0 < 𝛽< 1

Hence, the service time of a job is generally different from its intrinsic size 𝐿as the remaining
work is processed at the slower rate 𝛽once the memory threshold is crossed. In LLM inference, this
slowdown represents the loss of effective decoding throughput when the KV cache can no longer be
maintained entirely in GPU memory. Practical serving systems may respond to memory pressure
by swapping KV cache blocks to host memory, evicting cache state, or recomputing evicted state
later. These mechanisms introduce additional data movement and computation, which reduce the
effective rate at which decode work is completed. Rather than modeling these low-level operations
explicitly, 𝛽captures their aggregate effect on service speed.
2.3
Preemption and Switching Cost
The 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽model permits preemptive scheduling, but preemption is not assumed to be free.
When a job 𝑖is preempted after receiving 𝑎𝑖(𝑡) units of service and later resumed, its previously
accumulated memory states must be restored. We model this restoration overhead as an additional
service requirement proportional to the memory footprint at the time of preemption:
𝑐𝑖(𝑡) = 𝛾𝑔(𝑎𝑖(𝑡)),
(4)
where𝛾≥0 denotes the restoration cost per unit of accumulated state. We make one key assumption
for analytical tractability.
Assumption 1. Only one job is served at a time and only the memory of the running job is
retained in the server.


--- Page 6 ---
6
Jiahui Ni and Vishrant Tripathi
Therefore, preemption affects the queue through additional workload assigned to the preempted
job, but it does not create persistent memory pressure for future jobs. This separation is important
for ease of analysis: the memory-dependent slowdown experienced by a job is determined only
by its own attained service while it is running, whereas preemption overhead is accounted for
separately through the additional work 𝛾𝑔(𝑎𝑖(𝑡)). For LLM serving, preempting a request may
require its KV cache to be removed from GPU memory and later restored through recomputation
or data movement. The amount of state that must be reconstructed/transferred grows with the
amount of KV cache generated, motivating a restoration cost proportional to attained service.
The parameters 𝑔(·), 𝐶, 𝛽, and 𝛾therefore capture four distinct aspects of the serving system: dy-
namic memory growth with attained service, finite fast-memory capacity, service-rate degradation
beyond that capacity, and preemption-induced restoration overhead, respectively. The resulting
𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽model preserves enough of the classical 𝑀/𝐺/1 structure to support queuing analysis
while incorporating the system effects that are central to memory-constrained LLM scheduling.

Lemma 3.1 characterizes the stability region of non-preemptive, size-unaware policies. Never-
theless, non-preemptive policies can suffer from severe head-of-line blocking, as a long request
may delay many shorter requests. This motivates preemptive policies that interrupt jobs with large
attained service and give priority to newly arriving jobs that may complete sooner. In our model,
however, preemption incurs a positive overhead. Consequently, any policy that preempts with
positive probability increases the effective mean service requirement and therefore has a strictly
smaller stability region than its non-preemptive counterpart. This loss in stability does not prevent
preemption from being beneficial: at light or moderate loads, the reduction in head-of-line blocking
can outweigh the additional preemption cost, yielding a smaller mean response time.
4
Scheduling Design
4.1
Motivation from Age-Based Scheduling
Under the zero-information setting considered in this work, the scheduler does not know the size
of an individual job upon arrival. The attained service of a job therefore provides an important
source of information for scheduling decisions. Classical results for the 𝑀/𝐺/1 queue show that,
among work-conserving preemptive policies, the Gittins index policy minimizes mean response
time [9, 10]. The Gittins index of a job depends on its attained service and uses the conditional
distribution of its remaining size to determine its priority. Following the notations and definitions
used in [18], the efficiency function 𝐽(𝑎, Δ) for any Δ > 0 is defined as,
𝐽(𝑎, Δ) =
𝑃(𝑆−𝑎≤Δ|𝑆> 𝑎)
E[min{𝑆−𝑎, Δ}|𝑆> 𝑎],


--- Page 8 ---
8
Jiahui Ni and Vishrant Tripathi
where 𝑎denotes the attained service and Δ is the assigned quantum of service. 𝐽(𝑎, Δ) can be
interpreted as the ratio between the probability that a job with attained service 𝑎will complete
with a service quantum of Δ and the expected service time a job with attained service 𝑎and service
quantum Δ will require from the server. The Gittins index 𝐺(𝑎), 𝑎≥0 is defined as,
𝐺(𝑎) = sup
Δ≥0
𝐽(𝑎, Δ).
For any 𝑎≥0, the optimum quantum of service Δ∗(𝑎) is defined as,
Δ∗(𝑎) = sup{Δ ≥0|𝐺(𝑎) = 𝐽(𝑎, Δ)}.
Therefore, for each job with attained service 𝑎, the Gittins index 𝐺(𝑎) returns its highest efficiency
ratio achieved by the optimum quantum of service Δ∗(𝑎).
According to Theorem 2 and Definition 2 in [18], the Gittins index policy at every decision epoch
picks the job with the highest index value 𝐺(𝑎) and assigns it a service quantum Δ∗(𝑎). The next
decision epoch takes place once the previously selected job has received Δ∗(𝑎) units of service, or
when the previously selected job completes its service, or when a new job arrives at the queue.
Note that unlike the classical model, preemption is not work-conserving in the 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queue
and the Gittins index policy might cause the queue to be unstable under special assumptions on
the service time distribution.
Let’s define the hazard rate of a service time distribution as ℎ(𝑥) = 𝑓(𝑥)
¯𝐹(𝑥), where ¯𝐹(𝑥) = 1 −𝐹(𝑥)
is the complementary cumulative distribution function of the service time distribution. A service
time distribution belongs to the class Decreasing Hazard Rate (DHR) if ℎ(𝑥) ≥ℎ(𝑦) whenever
𝑥≤𝑦. It has a strictly decreasing hazard rate if the inequality is strict.
Lemma 4.1 (Instability of the classical Gittins rule under costly preemption). Assume
that the service time distribution has a strictly decreasing hazard rate. If a new job with size greater
than 𝑎> 0 arrives when an unfinished job is in service with attained service 𝑎, then the classical
Gittins-index policy induces infinitely many preemptions in the 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queue and causes the queue
to be unstable.
Proof. According to Proposition 5 in [18], the Gittins index for a DHR service-time distribution
is given by 𝐺(𝑎) = ℎ(𝑎). Since the hazard rate is assumed to be strictly decreasing, 𝐺(𝑎) is strictly
decreasing in the attained service 𝑎. Moreover, under strict DHR, the efficiency function 𝐽(𝑎, Δ)
is strictly decreasing in the service quantum Δ according to Proposition 1 in [18], so the optimal
Gittins service quantum satisfies Δ∗(𝑎) = 0.
Suppose that a job 𝑖is in service with attained service 𝑎> 0 when a new job 𝑗arrives. Since
𝐺(0) > 𝐺(𝑎), job 𝑗immediately receives priority. On the event that 𝑗does not complete before
receiving 𝑎units of service, the two unfinished jobs eventually satisfy 𝑎𝑖= 𝑎𝑗= 𝑎. At this instant
their Gittins indices are equal.
Now suppose that, because the server can serve only one job at a time, job 𝑖is selected. After
receiving any positive amount 𝜖> 0 of additional service, its attained service becomes 𝑎+ 𝜖,
whereas job 𝑗remains at attained service 𝑎. Since 𝐺(·) is strictly decreasing, 𝐺(𝑎+ 𝜖) < 𝐺(𝑎),
and the Gittins rule therefore requires job 𝑖to be preempted in favor of job 𝑗. The same argument
applies symmetrically after job 𝑗receives any positive amount of service. Hence no job can receive a
strictly positive service quantum while preserving the Gittins priority ordering. An exact single-job
implementation therefore requires service quanta converging to zero and infinitely many switches
between the tied jobs.
In the classical costless-preemption model, this limiting behavior is interpreted as processor
sharing between jobs tied at the highest Gittins index. In the present model, however, every


--- Page 9 ---
Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
9
preemption incurs a positive overhead; when the service quantum approaches 0, the limiting
behavior cannot be interpreted as processor sharing between jobs at a reduced rate. Let 𝑐(𝑎) > 0
denote the preemption cost at attained service 𝑎(for example, 𝑐(𝑎) = 𝛾𝑔(𝑎) under proportional
recomputation cost). If 𝑁preemptions occur after the jobs reach attained service 𝑎, the accumulated
overhead is at least 𝑁𝑐(𝑎). Since an exact implementation requires 𝑁→∞, an unbounded amount
of server work is spent on preemption overhead before any positive amount of useful service can
be completed beyond the tie state. Therefore, once such a state is reached, the involved jobs have
infinite response time. If this state is reachable with positive probability, the system admits no
stable stationary regime under a direct implementation of the classical Gittins-index policy.
□
Previous work [19, 20] has shown that multi-level scheduling policies with age-based priority
thresholds can perform within a constant factor of the Gittins index policy under costless preemption.
Therefore, to limit the preemption overhead, it is natural to use a multi-level policy with age-based
thresholds, and serve the job in each level non-preemptively and preempt the job only when it is
demoted to a lower priority level after reaching the attained-service thresholds. This preserves the
benefit of prioritizing jobs that are more likely to finish to mitigate head-of-line blocking, while
limiting the accumulated preemption overhead.
4.2
Mean Response Time of the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) Policy
We propose the following Multi-Level Priority Thresholds (MLPT)-(𝜃,𝑘) policy to balance the
trade-off between head-of-line blocking and preemption overhead through limited preemption.
The structure of the MLPT policy is strongly motivated by classical MLFQ scheduling [22], the
discretized foreground-background (FB) policy analyzed in [28], and preemption checkpointing as
discussed in [21]. The MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy consists of 𝑘priority levels, denoted by 𝑄1,𝑄2, . . . ,𝑄𝑘,
with strict priority 𝑄1 ≻𝑄2 ≻· · · ≻𝑄𝑘.
Jobs in the same level are served in an FCFS order. A newly arriving job enters 𝑄1. For 𝑖=
1, . . . ,𝑘−1, a job in 𝑄𝑖receives at most 𝜃units of service. If it does not complete within this
quantum, it is preempted at attained service 𝑖𝜃and demoted to 𝑄𝑖+1. Jobs reaching 𝑄𝑘are served
until completion. Therefore, a job can be preempted at most 𝑘−1 times when 𝑘is finite. We use
𝑘= ∞to denote the policy that allows a job to be demoted infinitely.
We assume that the attained service of a job does not include the preemption overheads needed
to reschedule the job, and that a preempted job is always rescheduled successfully. A job in 𝑄𝑖is
rescheduled only if there are no higher-priority jobs in the system, but once it resumes service, it is
non-preemptible until the allocated 𝜃units of service are exhausted.
Remark 1. In the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy, we assume that when a job reaches 𝜃units of service, it
is preempted proactively, independently of whether there are jobs in higher-priority levels in the
system. In other words, even if the system is empty, the job is preempted, demoted to 𝑄𝑖+1, and
rescheduled immediately, which always incurs a preemption overhead.
This simplifies the theoretical analysis, as the preemption overhead is entirely determined by the
original service requirement of the job and independent of the arrival process. While it is natural
to expect a practical scheduler to only preempt the job in service when there are new arrivals,
such a scheduler is equivalent to our proposed policy if we let the preemption overhead be zero if
𝑄1, ...𝑄𝑖+1 are all empty when a job in 𝑄𝑖attains 𝜃units of service. The fraction of time that the
preemption overhead is zero is small if we consider reasonably large values of 𝜃and a moderately
large system load. Therefore, our proposed policy has a mean response time close to the policy
with arrival-dependent preemptions while remaining analytically tractable.
The complete specification of the scheduling policy is detailed in Algorithm 1. We will next derive
the stability condition and the mean response time of the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy. Let 𝐹𝑆(𝑥) = Pr(𝑆> 𝑥)

Theorem 4.5 provides a useful expression for optimizing the mean response time with respect to
𝜃. For simplicity, we assume equal quantum 𝜃for each priority level in our analysis, so the optimal
quantum 𝜃∗can be obtained by solving a one-dimensional optimization problem, if 𝑘is given. It is
also convenient to extend our analysis to consider different quanta at each priority level. We can
denote the quantum at priority level 𝑖as 𝜃𝑖for 𝑖∈{1, 2, ...,𝑘−1}, and let the jobs in the last level 𝑘
serve to completion. So, we can represent the policy by a (𝑘−1)-dimensional vector 𝜽∈R𝑘−1
≥0 , and
solve a (𝑘−1)-dimensional optimization problem to optimize the mean response time.


--- Page 14 ---
14
Jiahui Ni and Vishrant Tripathi
While we note in Section 3 that any policy that preempts with positive probability increases
the effective mean service requirement and has a smaller stability region than its non-preemptive
counterpart, by optimizing 𝜃, the stability region of MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) can be made arbitrarily close to the
stability region of non-preemptive policies. Consider a base load 𝜌′
0 arbitrarily close to 1, making
any policy incurring positive preemption overhead unstable. Then at 𝜌0 = 𝜌′
0, selecting 𝜃= 0 or
𝜃= ∞will reduce the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) to FCFS, and thus remain stable. For any 𝜌0 < 𝜌′
0, optimizing 𝜃
will yield a smaller or equal mean response time for MLPT-(𝜃∗,𝑘) than FCFS. Therefore, optimizing
𝜃∗ensures that MLPT-(𝜃∗,𝑘) always has a smaller or equal mean response time as FCFS for any 𝜌0.
4.3
Finding the optimal 𝜃for MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘)
Finding a closed-form expression for the optimal 𝜃that minimizes the mean response time in Theo-
rem (4.5) is challenging for general service time distributions and requires numerical optimization.
In this section, we aim to propose rules of thumb for selecting an approximate optimal value of 𝜃
to yield a low mean response time of the proposed MLPT policy for 𝑘= 2 and 𝑘> 2. To simplify
calculation, we assume 𝑔(𝑟𝜃) = 𝑟𝜃in the following discussion.
The number of levels 𝑘determines the granularity of the scheduler. In the simplest setting where
we limit the number of priority levels to 𝑘= 2, the mean response time in Theorem 4.5 can be
written more explicitly as a function of 𝜃.
Corollary 4.6 (Mean response time of the MLPT-(𝜃, 2) policy).
E[𝑇(𝜃)] = E[𝑆eff

how the memory threshold ℓ𝐶affects the choice of quantum. For the smaller memory threshold,
ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿], the jump crosses the hazard curve, and there are no smaller below-to-above crossings

a candidate quantum 𝜃smaller than ℓ𝐶, and the jump at ℓ𝐶produces no additional sign change.
(a) ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿]
(b) ℓ𝐶= 8E[𝐿]
Fig. 3. Intersections of 𝐴(𝑥)
𝐵(𝑥) and ℎ𝐿(𝑥) for small and large ℓ𝐶, where 𝐿∼LogNorm(5, 0.92), 𝛽= 0.39, 𝛾= 0.1,
𝜆= 0.0036.
These examples suggest that when ℓ𝐶is small, ℓ𝐶itself can be a strong candidate for the optimal
quantum. Intuitively, when ℓ𝐶is small, preempting earlier than ℓ𝐶may cause frequent unnecessary
preemptions for small jobs that are likely to finish before the slowdown starts, while preempting
later than ℓ𝐶lets long jobs receive some slow service before being preempted, which would delay
the service of the waiting small jobs. Figure 4 and Figure 5 illustrate the impact of 𝛽and 𝛾on
the optimal quantum for small and large ℓ𝐶. When ℓ𝐶is large, larger 𝛾and smaller 𝛽encourage
choosing a larger quantum; when ℓ𝐶is small, the impact of ℓ𝐶dominates the choice of quantum, as
more jobs encounter the slowdown. However, when ℓ𝐶is very small, choosing 𝜃= ℓ𝐶causes a large
fraction of jobs to require preemption, adding overhead to a system already burdened by prolonged
service in the slow-service region. Increasing 𝜃reduces the fraction of jobs requiring preemption;
when this benefit outweighs the higher cost per preemption and the additional delay from longer
first-level service, the optimal quantum lies above ℓ𝐶. Therefore, there would be a lower and upper
bound for ℓ𝐶for it to be a useful threshold for preemption in the two-level policy.
Although two levels limit each job to at most one preemption, they also limit the scheduler’s
ability to distinguish jobs after their initial service period. Once a job enters the second level,
it is served nonpreemptibly to completion. A job with a large remaining service requirement

can therefore block subsequent arrivals, including short jobs. Increasing 𝜃reduces the remaining
second-level work of each surviving job and allows more jobs to finish without preemption, but
also delays the opportunity to give waiting jobs priority and incurs higher preemption overhead
for the preempted jobs. Consequently, a single boundary must balance several competing effects.
Allowing 𝑘> 2 provides additional opportunities to reassign priority as jobs accumulate service,
postponing entry into the terminal, nonpreemptible level until age (𝑘−1)𝜃. This can reduce the
blocking caused by long jobs. The benefit comes at the cost of additional overhead. A job with
service requirement 𝑆undergoes 𝑁demotions and incurs a total preemption overhead of

This approximation captures the inverse dependence of cumulative overhead on the quantum.

Our rule of thumb provides interesting insights on how to set the quantum 𝜃given the system
parameters. Intuitively, a larger cost factor𝛾favors a larger quantum 𝜃and less frequent preemption.
b𝜃also suggests the memory threshold ℓ𝐶as a useful threshold when only two priority levels are
allowed under limited memory space. With larger ℓ𝐶and higher scheduler granularity, the impact
of memory-induced slowdown ℓ𝐶and 𝛽is addressed implicitly in E[𝑆], E[𝑆2], and 𝜌0. Notably, the
second-moment dependence reflects the cumulative overhead of preemption costs proportional to
attained service. In Appendix B, we plot 𝜃∗and b𝜃under varying system parameters and arrival
rates. The result shows that b𝜃follows the trends in 𝜃∗as the system parameters vary, supporting
our proposed rule of thumb as a reasonable placeholder for 𝜃∗.
5
Numerical Simulations
In this section, we evaluate scheduling policies in the 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queue using mean response
time as the performance metric. Unless otherwise stated, the intrinsic job size follows 𝐿∼
LogNormal(5, 0.92), the slowdown factor is 𝛽= 0.39, and the preemption-cost factor is 𝛾= 0.1.
Each simulation measures the response times of 100,000 jobs following 20,000 warm-up arrivals.
Results are averaged over eight independent random seeds, using matched arrival and job-size
traces across policies. Error bars represent one standard error across the eight seed means.
As the stability and the mean response time of the proposed MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy depend on the
choice of quantum 𝜃and the number of priority levels 𝑘, we will first evaluate how the mean
response time of MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy varies with 𝜃and 𝑘, and compare it with FCFS. For these
simulations, we set the slowdown factor 𝛽= 0.39, the preemption cost factor𝛾= 0.1, and the arrival
rate 𝜆= 0.0036. Figure 6 shows the mean response time of MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) and FCFS for 𝑘= 2, 5, 10, ∞
when the memory threshold ℓ𝐶= 6E[𝐿], corresponding to a base load 𝜌0 = 𝜆E[𝑆] ≈0.8233. We
can observe that at 𝜃= 0, MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) is reduced to FCFS for finite 𝑘. At 𝜃∗, MLPT-(𝜃∗, 2) decreases
the mean response time by 21.7% and MLPT-(𝜃∗, ∞) decreases the mean response time by 32.2%
compared to FCFS. This shows the performance gain from increasing the priority levels in the
scheduler. At b𝜃given by the proposed rule of thumb, MLPT-(b𝜃, ∞) decreases the mean response

reduces the mean response time by 46.6% compared to FCFS, while MLPT-(𝜃∗, ∞) reduces the mean

gain of the MLPT-(𝜃∗,𝑘) with different priority levels 𝑘also suggests that increasing the scheduler

small, a single preemption improves upon the FCFS policy significantly, and increasing the priority
levels does not improve the performance of the MLPT-(𝜃∗, 2) policy by much. When the memory
capacity is large, increasing the scheduler granularity leads to more performance gain. We can
also observe that the mean response time of MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) converges to the mean response time of
MLPT-(𝜃, ∞) as 𝑘increases in the stable range of 𝜃, suggesting that the mean response time of
MLPT-(𝜃, ∞) can be approximated with MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) with finite 𝑘.
The curves labeled as MLPT′-(𝜃, ∞) in Figure 6, Figure 7, and Figure 8 show the mean response
time of the MLPT-(𝜃, ∞) policy when we remove the assumption in Remark 1; that is, when a job
has attained 𝑖𝜃units of service and demoted to 𝑄𝑖+1, the preemption overhead is incurred only
if there are jobs with higher priorities in the system. We observe that the mean response time of
MLPT′-(𝜃, ∞) is very close to the mean response time of MLPT-(𝜃, ∞). This supports our claim
that despite the simplification in the analysis of the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy, the mean response time of
the MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) policy is a close approximation of the mean response time of its counterpart with
arrival-dependent preemption under heavy load.
Figure 9 compares the mean response time of MLPT-(𝜃∗, 2) and MLPT-(𝜃∗, ∞) against FCFS and
other benchmark policies under different base loads 𝜌0, where we vary the arrival rate 𝜆and keep
E[𝑆] fixed. We use Capped Gittins (𝑘) as an age-based scheduling benchmark, where we apply the
Gittins Index policy, but limit the total number of preemptions of each job to at most (𝑘−1) times,
to avoid instability. Figure 9 shows that when the base load is low, all policies have comparable
performance. As the base load gets higher, the mean response time of Capped Gittins (𝑘) surges
and becomes worse than the mean response time of FCFS. The last data point of Capped Gittins
(3) is omitted as the simulation becomes unstable at the highest base load. On the other hand,
MLPT-(𝜃∗, 2) and MLPT-(𝜃∗, ∞) remain stable under heavy loads with much lower increase in the
mean response time than FCFS and Capped Gittins (𝑘).

6
Conclusion
In this work, we introduced the 𝑀/𝐺𝑔/1𝐶
𝛽queue, a new model for inference workloads with dynam-
ically growing memory footprints, finite memory capacity, memory-dependent service degradation,
and nonzero preemption overhead. Using this model, we characterized the fundamental stability
implications of memory constraints and the scheduling tradeoffs created by costly preemption.
We showed that the classical Gittins-index policy can incur substantial preemption overhead, and
proposed the MLPT policy to limit preemption while retaining priority for jobs with small attained
service. We derived the mean response time under MLPT and also proposed an empirical rule of
thumb for setting the quantum.
For future work, we plan to relax the assumption that only a single job runs inference at a
time. This will allow us to capture multiple servers sharing a common memory capacity and the
interaction between batching, scheduling, and memory contention. We also plan to allow preempted
jobs to retain their state in local memory. This can avoid transfer and recomputation overhead
upon resumption, but reduce the memory available to other jobs and may increase their service
times. On the implementation side, we plan to explore how our analytical insights and MLPT style
scheduling can be integrated into LLM inference serving systems in practice.

B
Optimal quantum 𝜃with varying system parameters
Figure 10 shows how the optimal quantum 𝜃∗for MLPT-(𝜃,𝑘) varies with ℓ𝐶, 𝛽, and 𝛾, comparing
𝑘= 2 and 𝑘= ∞at a fixed arrival rate 𝜆= 0.0036. For the 𝛽and 𝛾sweeps, we consider a small-
memory setting, ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿], and a large-memory setting, ℓ𝐶= 8E[𝐿]. Figure 10a shows that
both policies require a large quantum when ℓ𝐶is very small. In this regime, memory-induced
slowdown increases job service requirements and pushes the base load close to saturation, leaving
little capacity for preemption overhead. For ℓ𝐶< 3.5E[𝐿], the infinite-level policy selects a larger
quantum than the two-level policy, consistent with the need to control repeated preemptions of
long jobs. The two-level policy incurs this cost at most once per job. As ℓ𝐶increases, slowdown
and cumulative overhead become less restrictive, and the ordering eventually reverses. Additional
priority levels allow moderately sized jobs to retain priority over longer jobs after leaving the first
level, enabling the infinite-level policy to use a smaller quantum. In contrast, the two-level policy
benefits from allowing more jobs to finish before entering its final, nonpreemptible level.
The 𝛽and𝛾sweeps further illustrate this tradeoff. For ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿], the two-level optimum remains
at ℓ𝐶throughout the tested 𝛾range and most of the tested 𝛽range. The infinite-level optimum
decreases with 𝛽and increases with 𝛾, with a plateau at ℓ𝐶over part of each sweep. Increasing 𝛽
reduces the service requirements of jobs entering the slowdown region, lowering both the base


--- Page 23 ---
Queuing for Inference: Dynamic Memory Footprints and Costly Preemption
23
load and the number of quantum boundaries crossed by long jobs. Increasing 𝛾makes preemptions
more expensive and therefore favors a larger quantum. For ℓ𝐶= 8E[𝐿], both policies select smaller
quanta as 𝛽increases and larger quanta as 𝛾increases, with the infinite-level optimum consistently
below the two-level optimum. Together, these results suggest that the memory boundary can
anchor the optimal quantum under limited memory, while with more memory, the balance between
priority separation and preemption overhead becomes more prominent. Figure 10 also shows how
our proposed rule of thumb for the optimal quantum b𝜃varies with the system parameters. We
observe that b𝜃closely follows the trends in 𝜃∗as the system parameters vary.
These observations support our proposed rule of thumb in Section 4.3.
(a) 𝜃∗, b𝜃vs ℓ𝐶, 𝛽= 0.39, 𝛾= 0.1
(b) 𝜃∗, b𝜃vs 𝛽, ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿], 𝛾= 0.1
(c) 𝜃∗, b𝜃vs𝛾,ℓ𝐶= 3E[𝐿], 𝛽= 0.39
(d) 𝜃∗, b𝜃vs 𝛽, ℓ𝐶= 8E[𝐿], 𝛾= 0.1
(e) 𝜃∗, b𝜃vs𝛾,ℓ𝐶= 8E[𝐿], 𝛽= 0.39
Fig. 10. 𝜃∗for MLPT-(𝜃, 2) and MLPT-(𝜃, ∞) with varying ℓ𝐶, 𝛽, and 𝛾, where 𝐿∼LogNorm(5, 0.92), 𝜆=
0.0036.
